opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is: don't work on LLMs. Not because they're useless; they're very useful. But that's a game for industry right now. There are huge teams with enormous compute budgets working on scaling them up, fine-tuning them, and doing RLHF. A PhD student in a university lab is not going to make a big contribution by trying to compete with that. You're going to be outgunned.

What academia should do is work on the next thing, the stuff that's going to matter in five or ten years. In my opinion, that means figuring out how to get machines to understand the physical world. Current systems are trained on text, and text is a very impoverished representation of reality. A four-year-old child has seen more data through vision than the biggest LLMs have been trained on in text. Yet we don't have systems that can learn how the world works just by watching it, the way babies and animals do.

So there's a whole set of open problems. How do you build world models that can predict the consequences of actions? How do you learn good abstract representations from video and other sensory data? That's what we've been working on with joint embedding predictive architectures, JEPA, where you predict in representation space rather than trying to predict every pixel. How do you get systems that can plan and reason, not by generating tokens autoregressively, but by searching for a sequence of actions that optimizes an objective? How do you do hierarchical planning, where you plan at different levels of abstraction? Nobody really knows how to do that yet. How do you build systems with persistent memory?

None of those problems necessarily require gigantic compute to make progress, at least at the conceptual level. You can have a good idea, test it on a reasonable scale, and show that it works. That's exactly the kind of thing academia is good at. Many of the most important ideas in deep learning came from small groups with modest resources.

The other thing I'd say is that open-source models help a lot here. If academics have access to good open foundation models, they can build on them and study them without having to train everything from scratch. That's one of the reasons I've been such a strong advocate for open research and open platforms. It keeps the whole ecosystem healthy and allows universities to keep contributing.

So my advice is to be a little contrarian. Don't follow the crowd. Look for what's missing in current systems, and there's a lot missing, and work on that.

r001.rationale: It advises academics and PhD students not to compete on current LLMs, but to work on the next generation of AI systems and problems that will matter in the future.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I tell students is: don't work on LLMs. I mean that seriously. If you're a PhD student today, you're not going to beat the big industry labs at scaling up language models. They have thousands of GPUs, they have enormous teams, they have the data. Whatever incremental improvement you can make in that space, they can make faster. And frankly, I think LLMs are a bit of an off-ramp. They're useful, they're impressive in some ways, but they are not the path to human-level intelligence. So I don't think that's where the interesting scientific questions are anymore.

What I think students should work on is the next thing. And to me the next thing is figuring out how to get machines to learn how the world works the way humans and animals do. Think about a cat. A cat has maybe 800 million neurons, far fewer than any of these giant models, and yet a cat understands intuitive physics, it can plan, it can navigate complex environments, it knows that when it jumps on a shelf it's going to land. We have no AI system today that comes anywhere close to that. A ten-year-old can learn to clear the dinner table in one shot. A teenager learns to drive in twenty hours. We can't do either of those things with current systems, despite having essentially unlimited data for the self-driving case. So the question of why that is, that's a scientific question, and it's wide open.

So concretely, I'd say there are a few directions. One is learning world models from sensory input, from video, from observation, in a self-supervised way. Not predicting pixels, because that's a losing game, the world is too unpredictable at the pixel level. Instead, learning abstract representations where prediction becomes possible. That's the idea behind JEPA, joint embedding predictive architectures, and I think there's a huge amount of work to do there, both theoretically and practically.

A second direction is planning and reasoning that doesn't go through a token-by-token generation process. Current systems reason by generating text and checking it, which is a very weak form of reasoning. Real reasoning should be an optimization in an abstract space. How do you do that? How do you make it tractable? Nobody really knows yet.

Third is persistent memory, and the fourth is hierarchical planning, the ability to decompose a complex task into subgoals at multiple levels of abstraction, which is something humans do effortlessly and which we really don't know how to learn from data.

And the nice thing about these problems for an academic is that they don't require ten thousand GPUs. You can make real conceptual progress with modest compute, because the question isn't about scale, it's about what the right architecture and the right learning objective are. That's exactly the kind of problem where a clever idea from a student can change the field. That's historically where the big breakthroughs have come from. Nobody told us to work on convolutional nets or backprop when those were unfashionable.

So my advice is, don't follow the crowd. The crowd is in industry, working on something that's going to be commoditized in a couple of years. Go work on the hard problems that nobody has solved. That's what a PhD is supposed to be for.

r001.rationale: It advises students not to work on current LLMs and instead to pursue “the next thing,” including learning how machines can model the world.

astra-6.text:
I think researchers in academia, particularly PhD students, should work on ideas that are unlikely to be pursued in industry. If you work on exactly the same thing as a large industrial lab, and your success depends on having more computing resources, you’re putting yourself at a disadvantage. Your advantage is the freedom to question the assumptions everyone else is making.

So pick an important problem where we don’t yet know how to make progress. How do we get machines to learn how the world works from observation? How do we get them to reason and plan, to build representations that allow them to predict the consequences of their actions? How do we get them to learn with much less supervision?

These are questions where a good idea can matter more than the size of your computer cluster. And a PhD is an opportunity to take that kind of risk. Don’t choose a topic just because it’s popular. Work on something you think is missing, and develop enough conviction to explore it—even if it isn’t what everyone else is doing.

r001.rationale: The response recommends pursuing important, underexplored problems and gives examples such as learning how the world works, reasoning, and planning. It does not clearly characterize these as next-generation systems in contrast to current-generation systems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think researchers in academia should work on the questions that industry is neglecting. If you’re a PhD student, don’t just work on whatever everybody else is working on because it’s fashionable. Ask yourself what important problem is missing a good solution, and what ideas you have that might change how we approach it.

In AI, there are still very basic questions. How do we build systems that learn how the world works from observation? How do we give them persistent memory, the ability to reason, and the ability to plan? How do we get them to learn new tasks without requiring enormous amounts of supervision or trial and error?

Those are questions where academia can have a tremendous impact. You don’t necessarily need to train the largest model to test a new principle. You need a good idea and an experiment that tells you whether that idea is right.

So my advice is: take risks. Work on something that might fail, but that would matter if it succeeded. The value of academic research is precisely that you can explore directions whose payoff is uncertain and far away.

r001.rationale: The response recommends pursuing neglected, fundamental AI questions, but it does not clearly frame this as working on next-generation systems instead of current-generation systems.
